摘要
機器人移動式倉儲系統已成為滿足現代電子商務倉儲效率需求的變革性解 決方案。然而， SKU 與儲位的最佳化分配在考慮 SKU 差異性與實際儲存限制等 現實營運條件時，仍是一項關鍵挑戰。

本研究提出一套結構化、數據驅動的 SKU 分配策略，旨在在 RMFS 環境 中優化儲位空間利用率，同時提升訂單吞吐量與 Pile-On 表現。該方法將需求頻 率、產品週轉率、商品關聯性及尺寸可行性整合為一套統一的分類與配置策略。 首先，透過 K-means 分群法依據需求頻率對 SKU 進行分類，再以變異係數依需求 穩定性進一步細分。這些分類策略分別應用於三種配置情境：隨機分配、單倉單 類、單倉混類。為進一步提升可存取性，本研究引入分散策略，將高需求 SKU 分 散至多個儲位。研究透過 NetLogo 建立模擬模型，並結合 Python 最佳化模組，在 尺寸限制條件下及加入分散策略後評估各情境的效能表現。

結果顯示，在尺寸限制條件下，「單倉混類」策略表現最佳，訂單吞吐率 達 91.90% ， Pile-On 為 9.79 ，其次為「單倉單類」與「隨機分配」。引入分散策 略後，各情境的兩項效能指標均有進一步提升，其中「單倉混類」策略的吞吐率 提升至 99.22% ， Pile-On 提升至 9.96 。 ANOVA 檢定結果顯示，在尺寸限制及分散 策略下，三種情境在吞吐率與 Pile-On 上的差異均具有統計顯著性。成對 t 檢定進 一步驗證，分散策略對所有情境的兩項效能指標均帶來統計上顯著的改善。研究 結果證明，將基於需求的分類方法與分散策略及尺寸可行性結合，能夠在 RMFS 環境中實現更有效的 SKU 與儲位分配。
關鍵詞：機器人移動式倉儲系統、 SKU 分配、儲位分配、變異係數、尺寸限制、 混合策略、分散策略、訂單吞吐量、 Pile-On 。
ABSTRACT

Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems have emerged as a transformative solution to meet the efficiency demands of modern e-commerce warehouses. Yet, the optimization of SKU-to-pod assignment remains a critical challenge, especially when considering realworld operational constraints such as SKU variability and physical storage limitations.

This research proposes a structured, data-driven SKU allocation policy aimed at optimizing pod space utilization while improving throughput and pile-on performance in RMFS environments. The methodology integrates demand frequency, product turnover, item correlation, and dimensional feasibility into a unified classification and placement strategy. SKUs are first categorized by demand frequency using K-means clustering, and further  classified  based  on  demand stability using the Coefficient of Variation. These classifications are applied under three allocation configurations: Random placement, One Pod One Class, and One Pod Mixed Class. To further enhance accessibility, a dispersion policy  is  introduced  to  distribute  SKUs  across  multiple  pods.  A  simulation  model developed  in  NetLogo,  combined  with  optimization  modules  in  Python,  evaluates performance under dimensional constraints and with the dispersion policy applied.

Results indicate that under dimensional  constraints,  the One Pod Mixed Class strategy achieved the highest performance, with throughput reaching 91.90% and pile-on 9.79, followed by One Pod One Class and the Random baseline. The introduction of the dispersion  policy  further  improved  both  metrics  across  all  scenarios,  with  throughput increasing to 99.22% and pile-on to 9.96 for Mixed Class. Statistical validation using ANOVA confirmed significant differences in throughput and pile-on among the three scenarios under both dimensional constraints and with the dispersion policy. Paired t-tests further verified that dispersion produced statistically significant improvements in both metrics  for  all  scenarios.  These  results  demonstrate  that  combining  demand-based classification with dispersion and dimensional feasibility leads to more effective SKUto-pod assignments in RMFS environments.

elements.text: CHAPTER 1 INTRODUCTION
1.1 Background and Motivation

The  e-commerce  sector  has  witnessed  exponential  growth  in  recent  years, significantly reshaping global retail operations and consumer purchasing behaviors. As of 2024, the global logistics market for e-commerce is estimated at approximately USD 500.76  billion,  with  projections  estimating  a  rapid  increase  to  USD  609.59 billion  in  2025,  and  exceeding  USD  3.7  trillion  by  2034,  reflecting  a  compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 22.3% [1]. This surge of expansion is primarily driven by the rising demand for fast, accurate, and technology-supported logistics services, especially in the B2C segment. 2.1 Robotic Mobile Fulfillment System (RMFS)

Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems have emerged as a transformative innovation in warehouse logistics, particularly within the e-commerce sector. Unlike traditional picker-to-parts  systems  where  workers  walk  through  aisles  to  retrieve  items  [23], RMFS follows a parts-to-picker approach, where autonomous mobile robots transport storage units called pods, directly to human-operated or automated picking stations [20]. Several studies have shown that incorporating RMFS into warehouse systems can  significantly  cut  down  picker  travel  time,  making  higher  picking  rates  more doable  compared  to  traditional  warehouse  setups  [24].  Today,  RMFS  is  widely adopted by leading companies such as Alibaba, JD.com, and Cainiao, significantly improving warehouse productivity and cost efficiency [25], [26], [27].

2.2 Decision Problem in RMFS

Merschformann et al. [21] structured the decisions problems in RMFS into several levels  of  warehouse  operation,  with  each  influencing  different  aspects  of  system performance. These decisions are categorized into three main levels: strategic, tactical, and operational, each with distinct objectives and time periods.

Strategic level decisions are made during the construction phase of the warehouse and  have  long-term  implications.  At  this  stage,  one  of  the  key  considerations  is workstation  placement,  which  involves  deciding  where  to  position  picking  and replenishment  stations  in  relation  to  the  storage  area.  Another  important  factor  is storage area dimensioning, which includes determining the overall size of the storage space, how it's divided into zones, and how aisles are arranged.

Tactical  decisions  in  an  RMFS  are  typically  made  at  the  beginning  of  an operational period, such as the start of a workweek, workday or shift. These decisions involve  determining  number  of  pods  per  SKU,  ratio  of  pick  and  replenishment stations, replenishment level, and resource reallocation. These tactical decisions help the  system  stay  agile  and  responsive  to  short-term  changes,  ensuring  smooth operations throughout the day or week.

Storage Assignment Problem

In  Robotic  Mobile  Fulfillment  Systems,  the  storage  assignment  problem  is  a critical decision problem in tactical level [21], significantly impacting the operational efficiency and throughput of fulfillment operations. It involves assigning SKUs to appropriate  pods  in  a  manner  that  enhances  overall  picking  performance,  reduces robot travel time, and improves system responsiveness. Unlike traditional warehouses where  items  are  placed  in  fixed  racks  and  retrieved  manually,  RMFS  involves dynamic  inventory  storage  and  retrieval  facilitated  by  AMRs,  making  storage decisions more complex and interdependent with system-wide performance factors.

A number of studies have investigated SAP in RMFS settings by focusing on SKU correlation and clustering-based placement strategies. For instance, Kim et al. [33] and Li et al. [34] explored storage assignment strategies that aim to maximize the correlation degree among SKUs, grouping frequently co-ordered items together in the same pods to reduce the number of pod visits per order. Mirzaei et al. [35] expanded on this approach by proposing an integrated cluster allocation policy that accounts for both  item  correlation  and  turnover  rates.  Similarly,  Yang  [36]  emphasized  item similarity as a basis for storage location assignment. However, all the abovementioned studies operate under the constraint that each SKU is assigned to only one pod or group, a design that may limit flexibility and reduce opportunities for optimization under dynamic order scenarios.

In contrast, recent studies have introduced scattered storage as a more flexible and efficient strategy. In this model, a single SKU can be stored across multiple pods, thereby significantly enhance picking efficiency and is suitable for RMFS warehouse. Xiang et al. [37] using historical order data addressed the small-scale item storage assignment problem under the scattered storage method and solved it using a CPLEX solver. Mirzaei  et  al.  [22]  proposed  a  correlated  dispersion  storage  policy  that integrates  SKU  correlation,  turnover  frequency,  and  dispersion  across  pods.  This approach  improves  picking  performance  by  ensuring  that  items  with  high  cooccurrence and turnover rates are accessible from multiple pods without excessive redundancy. Ma et al. [10] added a classification layer, distinguishing between bestselling  and  general-selling  items.  Their  model  incorporated  item  classification alongside  correlation and  scattered storage considerations to  devise  a  more comprehensive storage policy. Zhang et al. [38] further enriched the literature by accounting  for  human  factors.  Their  research  considered  picking  efficiency  and pickers'  physical  effort.  A  more  detailed  comparison  of  previous  studies  on  the storage assignment problem is presented in Table 2.1.

However, despite the valuable contributions, a critical limitation remains across all  the  aforementioned  studies:  they  did  not  explicitly  consider  the  physical dimensions of SKUs and the size constraints of compartments within pods when assigning SKUs to storage locations. In real-world RMFS environments, each pod is divided into compartments with fixed geometrical capacities, and SKUs vary in size and shape. Ignoring these crucial constraints can lead to theoretically optimal storage policies that are infeasible in practice. As such, solutions derived without considering volume fitting, dimension compatibility, and slot availability may not translate well into operational settings. Bridging this gap requires integrating physical feasibility checks into the storage assignment logic to ensure that assigned SKUs can actually be placed in the intended compartments.

2.3 Item Correlation

Item correlation is widely recognized as a crucial concept in modern warehouse optimization and plays an important role in solving the storage assignment problem within Robotic Mobile  Fulfillment Systems.  As  highlighted in the previous subchapter, many recent studies (see Table 2.1) use item correlation to improve SKUto-pod assignment strategies. When products with high correlation are placed together within the same pod, they are more likely to be appeared together in a single order [41]. This increases the number of items that can be retrieved in a single pod trip, thereby  reducing  the  overall  number  of  pod  visits  required  to  complete  order fulfillment.

By understanding how products are frequently ordered together, researchers and practitioners  can  identify  meaningful  relationships  that  helps  clustering,  scattered storage policies, and mixed storage configurations. This data-driven perspective helps RMFS warehouses boost picking efficiency, reduce unnecessary robot travel, and adapt dynamically to changing demand patterns.

Market  Basket  Analysis  is  one  of  the  most  widely  applied  techniques  for uncovering these item relationships that associated with customer buying behaviour [42]. MBA relies on Association Rule Mining to analyze transaction data, detecting which  items  appear  together  in  customer  orders.  Studies  such  as  Ünvan  [43] demonstrate that robust algorithms like Apriori and FP-Growth can effectively reveal strong correlations between SKUs. These patterns can then be used to group items with high co-occurrence, ultimately improving layout and storage allocation decisions in practice.

The  strategic  impact  of  understanding  item  correlation  extends  beyond  simple pairings.  Kumar  et  al.  [44]  emphasize  that  recognizing  hidden  interdependencies among SKUs enables companies to design smarter replenishment rules and crossselling  opportunities,  while  Sajwan  and  Tripathi  [45]  show  that  a  comprehensive MBA framework can illuminate the more complex interdependencies in shopping baskets,  allowing  companies  to  tailor  promotions,  manage  stock  levels,  and  even redesign store layouts to reflect actual buying behavior. Their study underscores the potential of ARM for generating strategic business insights, rather than treating it solely as a technical data mining task.

In the context of RMFS, association rules hold particular value for SKU-to-pod assignment and storage design. By identifying frequently co-ordered items, warehouse managers can cluster highly correlated SKUs within the same pods or strategically  disperse  them  to  balance  picking  efficiency  and  travel  distance.  The insights gained through ARM thus align closely with broader warehouse optimization goals, including increase order throughput and pile-on.
2.4 SKU Classification

Effective SKU classification is a fundamental component in optimizing storage strategies within RMFS. As modern warehouses handle thousands of diverse SKUs with  varying  demand  patterns,  dimensions,  and  turnover  rates,  classifying  SKUs appropriately enables more intelligent decisions in storage assignment, order picking, and replenishment planning. By grouping SKUs based on shared attributes such as demand frequency, volatility, or co-occurrence in orders, RMFS can achieve higher picking efficiency and reduce unnecessary pod movements.

Several  studies  have  highlighted  the  importance  of  SKU  classification  in improving warehouse performance, such as reduce pick travel distance and enhance throughput.    Yuan  et  al.  [46]  investigated  pod  assignment  strategies  in  RMFS  by comparing  random,  class-based,  and  turnover-based  approaches.  Their  findings indicate that class-based storage using two or three categories captures most of the potential advantages, with having more variation. Muppani and Adil [13] demonstrated that implementing a class-based storage policy, which groups SKUs with similar demand patterns, can reduce both order picking distance and required storage space. This approach improves space utilization and helps ensure that highturnover products are stored in more accessible locations. Another study by Mirzaei et  al.  [22]  demonstrated  that  combining  turnover-based,  correlation-based,  and dispersed storage strategies in robotic warehouses can lead to significant cost savings and  reduce  operational  time.  By  aligning  SKU  placement  with  both  demand frequency and product correlations, and distributing inventory across multiple pods, warehouses  can  reduce  retrieval  effort,  limit  pod  congestion,  and  improve  order fulfillment efficiency. This integrated approach minimizes unnecessary robot travel and redundant handling, resulting in lower operational costs.
2.5 Coefficient of Variation (CV)

In  order  to  effectively  manage  inventory  and  improve  storage  assignment  in Robotic Mobile Fulfilment Systems, it is important to recognize that not all SKUs behave the same in terms of demand. One way to capture this variability is through the  Coefficient  of  Variation,  a  statistical  measure  that  measures  the  ratio  of  the standard deviation to the mean of a data set [47]. The coefficient of variation is widely used across various fields such as agriculture, industry, healthcare, social sciences, and education, serving multiple research and analytical purposes [48]. In the context of  inventory  and  warehouse management, CV serves as a normalized indicator to quantify  the  volatility  of  SKU  demand,  providing  a  solid  foundation  for  setting differentiated inventory and storage allocation policy.

In an  RMFS  environment,  where  storage  space  is  mobile  and  dynamic, understanding the volatility of SKU demand is essential for optimizing SKU-to-pod assignments. This study applies CV as a decision variable to determine the inventory service level and the dispersion strategy for each SKU. SKUs with low CV values typically  show  stable  and  predictable  demand.  In  contrast,  SKUs  with  higher  CV values tend to display irregular or intermittent demand.

The  relevance  of  using  CV  for  classification  has  been  well-established  across various fields.  For  example,  the  ABC-XYZ  classification  framework,  which combines demand quantity (ABC) with demand variability (XYZ), applies the CV as a core measure to distinguish between stable (X class), moderately variable (Y-class), and highly erratic (Z class) items [49]. This combined approach helps companies align their inventory control and replenishment strategies with the real patterns of order.

Beyond warehousing, the value of CV as a simple yet robust analytical tools has also been demonstrated in fields such as agricultural monitoring, where it was used to classify cropland areas across diverse climates based on temporal backscatter data [50].  Taken  together,  these  examples  highlight  that  integrating  CV  into  SKU analytical tools enables more responsive, data-driven storage and inventory decisions, ultimately  supporting  higher  picking  efficiency  and  system  throughput  in  RMFS operations.

3.3.2 K-Means Clustering & Elbow Method

This  study  combines  K-Means  clustering  and  Elbow  method  to  determine  the number of SKU classes. K-means is a clustering algorithm that partitions data into K distinct groups by minimizing the distance between each data point and the center (centroid) of its assigned cluster [55]. Before applying the K-means algorithm, one important consideration is selecting an appropriate value for the number of clusters (K). One commonly used technique for determining this value is the Elbow method.

The elbow method identifies the optimal K by analyzing a graph that plots the Within-Clusters Sum of Squared (WCSS) against different K values (see Equation (34)) [56]. The ideal point is typically located at the "elbow" of the curve, where the SSE begins to level off. This point represents the best number of clusters to use.

In this study, three product mixture scenarios are considered to evaluate the impact of different allocation strategies on system performance:
a. Random placement (baseline)

Each  pod  contains  a  mix  of  SKUs  from  different  classification  groups.  This diversified allocation increases the probability that a single pod can fulfill a wider range of order lines, thereby improving the pile-on rate and reducing the total number of pod movements required for order fulfillment.

By analyzing these three SKU mixture scenarios, this study aims to identify the configuration that best balances inventory management complexity with operational efficiency, ultimately supporting higher throughput and pile-on.

3.6 SKU Dispersion

Scattered or dispersed storage has been widely recognized in the literature as an effective approach  to enhance  picking efficiency  in  warehouse  systems.  By distributing SKUs across multiple storage locations or pods, the likelihood of having required items closer to pick stations increases, thereby reducing travel distances and improving system responsiveness. As summarized in Chapter 2, Table 2.1, several studies  have  demonstrated  that  this  strategy  is  especially  beneficial  in  RMFS warehouse.

In this study, SKU dispersion is implemented based on the CV of each SKU's order  frequency.  The  CV  serves  as  a  normalized  measure  of  demand  variability, offering  a  standardized  basis  for  determining  how  widely  each  SKU  should  be distributed within the storage system. A higher CV indicates greater variability and unpredictability in order patterns, while a lower CV suggests more stable, consistent demand.

SKUs with high CV values are dispersed across a larger number of pods. This strategy increases the chances that SKUs whose demand patterns are sporadic, are available when needed, improving the system's responsiveness and reducing the risk of  pod  unavailability.  In  contrast,  SKUs  with  low  CV  values  exhibit  stable  and predictable demand and are therefore assigned to fewer pods to save storage space and avoids storing the same items unnecessarily.

3.8 Hypothesis Test

To verify whether the proposed SKU mixture and dimensional constraint strategies yield significantly different results compared to the baseline, a hypothesis test was conducted using two types of statistical method.

When comparing the means across three or more groups, the one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) is commonly employed as the appropriate statistical method [58]. The  ANOVA test evaluates  whether  there  are  significant  differences  between  the mean performance measures of the three different scenarios considered in this study. The null hypothesis ( 𝐻 ₀)  assumes that there is no significant difference in system performance among the scenarios, while the alternative hypothesis ( 𝐻 ₁) states that at least one scenario differs significantly, see Equation 3-17.

In  addition,  a  paired  t-test  was  used  to  compare  the  performance  between  the without dimensional constraints and with dimensional constraints scenarios. Since these two conditions are directly related and paired within each SKU mixture setting, the t-test provides an appropriate method to test for significant differences in means across paired groups [59]. The hypotheses are defined in Equation 3-18.

By analyzing the p-values obtained from both the ANOVA and t-test results, the null hypothesis can be either rejected or accepted, providing statistical validation for the observed differences in throughput and pile-on rates.
4.1 Data Preprocessing

The initial stage of this study involved data cleaning and preprocessing to ensure reliability and validity of the simulation input. The original SKU size dataset consists of 10,321 unique SKUs collected from the company's records. At first, all duplicate entries  and  null  values  were  identified  and  removed.  Furthermore,  SKUs  that exceeded the dimensional constraints of the pod compartments' size were filtered out and reassigned to a separate warehouse facility specifically designated for handling big sized items.

In parallel, the original order history dataset consists of 321,382 customer orders collected  over  a  21-day  operational  period  also  underwent  the  same  cleaning procedure to remove duplicates and null values. Additionally, SKUs associated with exceptionally  high  order  quantities  were  identified  and  allocated  for  split  order processing in different warehouse specifically designated for handling split orders.

Following these preprocessing stages, the cleaned SKU size and order datasets were  matched  to  ensure  consistency  between  two  datasets.  As  a  result,  the  final dataset consisted of 7,024 SKUs and 316,553 customer orders, providing a robust and realistic basis for the subsequent SKU to pod assignment simulation.

4.5 Application of SKU Dispersion

To improve picking efficiency, a SKU dispersion policy was applied based on both  the  SKU's  cluster  classification  and  its  Coefficient  of  Variation  (CV).  This policy determines how widely each SKU should be distributed across pods, while still considering physical constraints such as the available compartment space and the maximum capacity of the warehouse. The goal is to balance access speed for high-priority SKUs with the space limitations introduced by dimensional constraints.

Table  4.9  presents  the  dispersion  policy  assigned  to  each  subgroup  of  SKUs, categorized by their cluster label (A, B, C) and CV class (0, 1, 2). A higher dispersion value means the SKU is stored in more pods, enhancing accessibility and reducing retrieval time. For example, SKUs in Cluster A (high demand) are assigned higher dispersion  values  (up  to  6)  for  intermittent  demand  to  support  rapid  fulfillment. Similarly, SKUs in Cluster B (medium demand) receive moderate dispersion values, with intermittent SKUs dispersed across 4 pods.

On the other hand, Cluster C, which includes SKUs with low overall demand regardless of their CV value, is assigned the lowest dispersion level. Although SKUs in  this  cluster  have  high  CV  values  indicating  irregularity,  the  absolute  demand volume remains low. As such, a dispersion value of 1 is applied to minimize pod usage without significantly impacting operational performance.

4.6 Simulation Result

To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed SKU-to-pod assignment strategies, a simulation was conducted using the NetLogo platform. To ensure the reliability of the results, each scenario was replicated 5 times under the same configuration, and the average performance metrics were recorded. Each simulation was run for a total duration of 8 hours, with an order arrival rate of 300 orders per hour.

From the simulation outputs, two key performance indicators were computed for each scenario: throughput and pile-on rate. Both metrics were calculated using the formulas presented earlier in Chapter 3.
4.6.1 With Dimensional Constraints Throughput Performance

Table  4.12  presents  the  throughput  results  obtained  from  the  simulation  of scenarios without dimensional constraints, showing the throughput rate for each of the three SKU placement strategies across five replications along with their average values.
Table 4.  12 Throughput Results for Scenarios with Dimensional Constraints

Among the three scenarios, the One Pod Mixed Class configuration achieved the highest  performance,  with  an  average  throughput  of  91.90%  over  8  hours.  This scenario  consistently  outperformed  the  others  in  all  replications,  indicating  that allowing  multiple  demand  classes  to  share  the  same  pod  maximizes  compartment utilization and reduces the total number of pod visits required.

The One Pod One Class scenario followed with a mean throughput of 85.23%. Although lower than the mixed class configuration, this scenario still performed better than the Random assignment, which recorded the lowest average throughput at only 78.90%,  primarily  due  to  uneven  SKU  distribution  and  increased  pod  switching, which negatively impacted order fulfillment efficiency.
Pile-On Performance
Table  4.13  presents  the  pile-on  results  for  each  of  the  three  SKU  placement strategies across five replications in the simulation with dimensional constraints.
Table 4.  13 Pile-On Results for Scenarios with Dimensional Constraints

Among the three scenarios, the One Pod Mixed Class scenario again achieved the highest performance, with an average pile-on value of 9.79. This improvement can be attributed  to  the  diverse  SKU  composition  within  each  pod,  which  increases  the likelihood of fulfilling multiple order lines from a single retrieval. The One Pod One Class  scenario  followed  closely  with  an  average  pile-on  of  9.37,  benefiting  from demand-class grouping that maintains picking efficiency while reducing unnecessary pod exchanges. The Random scenario yielded the lowest pile-on rate at 7.35, which reflects lower picking efficiency due to scattered SKU distribution and less optimized pod mixture, resulting in more frequent pod visits for order fulfilment. This result indicating  that  mixing  SKUs  across  demand  classes  in  the  same  pods  not  only improves throughput but also enhances pod utilization.
4.6.2 Application of Dispersion
Throughput Performance

Table 4.14 shows the throughput results obtained from the simulation runs after applying  dispersion  in  the  SKU  mixture.  Each  scenario  was  tested  across  five replications using the same parameter as previous simulation.
Table 4.  14 Throughput Results for Scenarios with Dispersion Policy

After  applying  dispersion  policy,  the  One  Pod  Mixed  Class  configuration achieved the highest mean throughput at 99.22%, surpassing its previous performance of 91.90% under dimensional constraints. This improvement highlights how strategically dispersing SKUs enhances the likelihood of fulfilling more order lines from each pod visit, thereby reducing retrieval cycles and idle times.

The One Pod One Class scenario also demonstrated an increase, with average throughput rising from 85.23% to 96.22%. This gain indicates that combining classbased  grouping  with  calculated  dispersion  enables  a  more  balanced  allocation  of high-demand and volatile SKUs, supporting consistent picking efficiency.

The Random also scenario benefited from the dispersion policy, improving from 78.90% to 79.93%. However, the increase was marginal,  suggesting that without structured SKU  placement, dispersion alone cannot fully optimize system performance.
Pile-On Performance
Table  4.15  presents  the  pile-on  results  for  each  SKU  placement  strategy  after applying dispersion policy.
Table 4.  15 Pile-On Results for Scenarios with Dispersion Policy

The One Pod Mixed Class scenario achieved the highest mean pile-on value of 9.96, improving from previous performance at 9.79 under dimensional constraints. This increase indicates that the dispersion policy further concentrated relevant SKUs within pods, enabling a higher number of picks per pod visit.

Similarly, the One Pod One Class configuration improved from an average of 9.37 to  9.75,  showing  that  even  with  class-based  separation,  strategic  SKU  dispersion supports better fulfillment during picking operations.

The Random scenario also experienced a slight improvement, rising from 7.35 to 7.46, but the gain was minimal, suggesting that dispersion without a structured pod configuration has limited impact on pile-on efficiency.
4.7 Hypothesis Test

To statistically validate the simulation results, hypothesis testing was conducted to evaluate whether the differences observed between the SKU-to-pod strategies are statistically significant. ANOVA test was applied using Excel to both throughput and pile-on results to determine whether there are significant differences among the three scenarios: Random, One Pod One Class, and One Pod Mixed Class.

In addition, paired t-tests were performed to compare each scenario's performance with  dimensional  constraints  and  with  dispersion  policy.  This  analysis  aims  to identify whether the application of dimensional constraints and dispersion policy has a statistically significant impact on system performance in terms of throughput and pile-on.

5.1 Conclusion

The rapid rise of Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems has introduced numerous decision-making challenges aimed at improving order fulfillment efficiency. Among these, the optimization of the Storage Assignment Problem (SAP) has emerged as a critical  concern,  as  it  directly  affects  warehouse  performance.  While  a  variety  of performance  metrics  have  been  proposed  to  evaluate  SKU  allocation  strategies, maximizing throughput remains the main goal across all warehouse operations. Most research on SAP has primarily emphasized SKU correlation and item classification methods, which are indeed important for formulating allocation policies. However, such approaches often assume the presence of strong SKU relationships, which is not always the case in every warehouse. However, despite the valuable contributions, a critical  research  gap  remains  across  previous  studies,  they  did  not  consider  the physical dimensions of SKUs and the size constraints of compartments within pods when assigning SKUs to storage locations.

In this study, we proposed a SKU-to-pod allocation strategy specifically designed for RMFS warehouses, incorporating several key operational factors such as order frequency, product turnover rates, product correlation, and dimensional constraints. Our approach began with a systematic analysis of historical order data to classify SKUs  based  on  demand  frequency  and  stability.  We  proposed  two  SKU-to-pod policies  based  on  this  SKUs  classification:  one  pod  one  class  policy  and  one  pod mixed class policy, we then compared these two allocation policies with the random policy  baseline.  To  evaluate  the  real-world  applicability  of  the  proposed  policies, dimensional constraints were applied to all three scenarios. Furthermore, a dispersion policy was introduced to investigate the effect of distributing SKUs across multiple pods, thereby increasing SKU accessibility.  A simulation model was developed using NetLogo for agent-based modeling and Python for optimization, and performance was evaluated using a dataset of 7,024 SKUs.

Simulation results showed that under dimensional constraints alone, the One Pod Mixed  Class  strategy  achieved  the  best  performance,  with  mean  throughput  of 91.90%  and  mean  pile-on  of  9.79,  followed  by  One  Pod  One  Class  with  mean throughput of 85.23% and mean pile-on of 9.37 and the Random baseline with mean
CHAPTER 5 CONCLUSION

throughput of 78.65% and mean pile-on of 7.35. After applying the dispersion policy, both metrics improved across all scenarios. Mix Class scenario throughput increased to 99.22%, One Class scenario to 96.22%, and Random scenario to 79.93%, while pile-on rose to 9.96, 9.75, and 7.46, respectively. These gains coincide with greater storage  usage  from  roughly  273  to  472  pods,  reflecting  the  trade-off  between dispersion and pod capacity requirements.

Hypothesis  testing  using  ANOVA  confirmed  significant  differences  in  both throughput and pile-on across all scenarios under dimensional constraints and under the dispersion policy (p < 0.05). Paired t-tests further verified that introducing the dispersion policy led to statistically significant improvements in throughput and pileon for all three allocation strategies (p < 0.05).  These results validate the effectiveness of  SKU  classification  by  demand  frequency  and  stability,  and  demonstrate  that dispersion can further enhance performance by increasing SKU accessibility, while also highlighting the importance of considering physical storage constraints in realworld RMFS optimization.
5.2 Recommendation and Future Research

While this study has successfully proposed  a structured SKU-to-pod allocation policy and demonstrated significant improvements in both throughput and pile-on performance, several directions remain open for future exploration to further enhance RMFS operations.

The  current  classification  framework  is  primarily  based  on  demand  stability. However,  additional  factors  such  as  SKU  physical  size,  weight,  and  handling complexity  could  be  integrated  into  the  classification  criteria  to  create  more comprehensive storage profiles.

Future research could incorporate pod weight balancing when designing SKU-topod assignment policies. Uneven weight distribution within pods may increase the mechanical  burden  on  AMRs  and  negatively  affect  battery  efficiency  and  energy consumption. Introducing a weighted balancing constraint during SKU assignment could help ensure pod stability and improve the energy consumption of AMRs.

Continuing from previous recommendation, energy consumption is an increasingly important performance metric in modern warehouse systems. While this study focused on throughput and pile-on, future work could evaluate strategies based on energy efficiency, such as minimizing total robot travel distance or power usage, thus aligning system design with sustainability goals.

Finally,  a  promising  area  lies  in  developing  dynamic  SKU-to-pod  policies  that adapt in real time to changing demand patterns. As product lifecycles shorten and customer  preferences  fluctuate,  integrating  predictive  analytics  or  reinforcement learning,  future  systems  can  reconfigure  SKU  placements  periodically,  ensuring sustained efficiency under evolving operational conditions.

In  summary,  while  this  research  has  laid  a  solid  foundation  for  a  feasible  and effective  SKU  allocation  policy  in  RMFS,  future  enhancements  that  incorporate product-specific attributes, energy efficiency metrics, and real-time adaptability hold great potential to advance the state-of-the-art in intelligent warehouse automation. By building upon the groundwork established in this study and exploring the proposed extensions, future research can further drive the evolution of RMFS and contribute meaningfully to broader innovations in automated warehouse management.

本研究提出一套結構化、數據驅動的 SKU 分配策略，旨在在 RMFS 環境 中優化儲位空間利用率，同時提升訂單吞吐量與 Pile-On 表現。該方法將需求頻 率、產品週轉率、商品關聯性及尺寸可行性整合為一套統一的分類與配置策略。 首先，透過 K-means 分群法依據需求頻率對 SKU 進行分類，再以變異係數依需求 穩定性進一步細分。這些分類策略分別應用於三種配置情境：隨機分配、單倉單 類、單倉混類。為進一步提升可存取性，本研究引入分散策略，將高需求 SKU 分 散至多個儲位。研究透過 NetLogo 建立模擬模型，並結合 Python 最佳化模組，在
尺寸限制條件下及加入分散策略後評估各情境的效能表現。

Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems have emerged as a transformative solution to meet the efficiency demands of modern e-commerce warehouses. Yet, the optimization of SKU-to-pod assignment remains a critical challenge, especially when considering realworld operational constraints such as SKU variability and physical storage limitations.
This research proposes a structured, data-driven SKU allocation policy aimed at optimizing pod space utilization while improving throughput and pile-on performance in RMFS environments. The methodology integrates demand frequency, product turnover, item correlation, and dimensional feasibility into a unified classification and placement strategy. SKUs are first categorized by demand frequency using K-means clustering, and further  classified  based  on  demand stability using the Coefficient of Variation. These classifications are applied under three allocation configurations: Random placement, One Pod One Class, and One Pod Mixed Class. To further enhance accessibility, a dispersion policy  is  introduced  to  distribute  SKUs  across  multiple  pods.  A  simulation  model developed  in  NetLogo,  combined  with  optimization  modules  in  Python,  evaluates performance under dimensional constraints and with the dispersion policy applied.

Results indicate that under dimensional  constraints,  the One Pod Mixed Class strategy achieved the highest performance, with throughput reaching 91.90% and pile-on 9.79, followed by One Pod One Class and the Random baseline. The introduction of the dispersion  policy  further  improved  both  metrics  across  all  scenarios,  with  throughput increasing to 99.22% and pile-on to 9.96 for Mixed Class. Statistical validation using ANOVA confirmed significant differences in throughput and pile-on among the three scenarios under both dimensional constraints and with the dispersion policy. Paired t-tests further verified that dispersion produced statistically significant improvements in both metrics  for  all  scenarios.  These  results  demonstrate  that  combining  demand-based classification with dispersion and dimensional feasibility leads to more effective SKUto-pod assignments in RMFS environments.

The  e-commerce  sector  has  witnessed  exponential  growth  in  recent  years, significantly reshaping global retail operations and consumer purchasing behaviors. As of 2024, the global logistics market for e-commerce is estimated at approximately USD 500.76  billion,  with  projections  estimating  a  rapid  increase  to  USD  609.59 billion  in  2025,  and  exceeding  USD  3.7  trillion  by  2034,  reflecting  a  compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 22.3% [1]. This surge of expansion is primarily driven by the rising demand for fast, accurate, and technology-supported logistics services, especially in the B2C segment. The evolution of this market is illustrated in Figure 1.1, which shows the projected regional growth of e-commerce logistics from 2020 to  2034,  highlighting  the  dominant  role  of  North  America  and  the  fast-growing influence of Asia Pacific.

In  addition  to  major  e-commerce  players  like  Amazon,  a  growing  number  of department stores and supermarkets have also provided online shopping platforms. This widespread shift has significantly expanded the scale of distribution centers and delivery operations [2].

This rapid rise of e-commerce has been significantly accelerated by the COVID19 pandemic, which acted as a major catalyst for digital transformation in the retail sector. Widespread lockdowns and social distancing policies compelled many brick and mortar retailers to temporarily shut down physical stores, prompting an urgent shift toward digital commerce and technology-driven fulfillment solutions. This shift led to the rapid adoption of systems such as online ordering, click-and-collect services, and  robotics-assisted  operations  to  maintain  continuity  in  order  fulfillment  under restrictive conditions [3], [4].
Prior to the pandemic, traditional e-commerce fulfillment relied heavily on manual labor  for  handling  and  processing  orders[5].  However,  as  demand  surged  and efficiency requirements grew more stringent, many warehouses began transitioning toward automation [6]. Recent advancements in robotics have enabled the emergence of  hybrid  fulfillment  models  that  combine  human  labor  with  autonomous  agents, improving accuracy, scalability, and responsiveness [7], [8].

This transition toward automation has fundamentally transformed the logistics and warehousing  landscape,  but  it  has  also  introduced  new  operational  challenges. Modern e-commerce warehouses must now cope with a large assortment of SKUs, frequent small-batch orders, strict delivery windows, and highly variable workloads throughout the day [9]. One of the most labor-intensive and costly operations within a warehouse is order fulfillment, particularly the order picking process, the retrieval of items to complete customer orders which accounts for 55% of the total warehouse operating  expenses  [10],  [11],  [12].  Moreover,  only  about  40%  of  direct  labor activities  are  devoted  to  productive  tasks  like  loading,  unloading,  stocking,  and picking, whereas the remaining 60% is primarily spent on unproductive travel within the  warehouse  [13].  Due  to  these  rising  complexities  of  e-commerce  orders, traditional manual picking systems struggle to maintain efficiency. As a result, many warehouses have started integrating automation technologies, such as Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems, to optimize operations.

Wurman et al. [14] introduced a pioneering approach to warehouse automation, proposing the use of autonomous mobile robots to transport storage units, later termed 'pods',  to  designated  locations  known  as  'workstations,'  where  human  operators complete the picking process. This innovative system, which became widely known as the Kiva system, laid the foundation for a new generation of robotic fulfillment solutions [15], [16]. Since its initial deployment by Kiva systems in 2012 [17], the Robotic  Mobile  Fulfillment  System  has  gained  widespread  adoption  in  global  ecommerce warehouses.  Leading  companies  such  as  Amazon,  Walgreens,  Staples, JD.com,  and  Alibaba's  Cainiao  Network  have  integrated  RMFS  into  their  order fulfillment operations to enhance efficiency and scalability [18].

The  components  within  RMFS  are  highly  interdependent,  creating  a  complex operational  environment.  While  the  system  offers  massive  improvements  over traditional  warehousing  methods,  it  also  introduces  a  range  of  decision-making problems.  Research  on  RMFS  has  predominantly  focused  on  addressing  various optimization,  assignment,  and  scheduling  problems  to  enhance  overall  system performance [21].
While the optimization of RMFS has been extensively investigated by scholars in recent  years,  research  on  categorized  storage  remains  limited.  Current  studies primarily  focus  on  improving  robot  routing,  order  sequencing,  and  pod  retrieval strategies,  yet  the  fundamental  problem  of  efficient  SKU  allocation  to  storage locations has not received the same level of attention. In RMFS warehouses, the way SKUs  are  assigned  to  pods  significantly  impacts  retrieval  efficiency,  system throughput,  and  overall  warehouse  performance  [2].  A  poorly  optimized  SKU allocation strategy may lead to excessive pod retrievals, higher energy consumption and longer order fulfillment time.

Another critical issue in SKU-to-pod assignment is pile-on efficiency, which refers to the number of items that can be picked from a single pod visit. In an optimized RMFS, frequently co-ordered SKUs should be stored together in the same pod to reduce the number of pod retrievals per order [22]. Poor SKU placement disrupts this balance, forcing robots to retrieve multiple pods for a single order. Consequently, retrieval  delays  increase,  fulfillment  speeds  decline,  and  warehouse  throughput  is negatively affected.
In light of these challenges, this research specifically investigates the issue of SKU allocation  in  RMFS  warehouses,  aiming  to  assign  SKUs  to  pods  in  a  way  that maximizes  order  throughput  and  pile-on.  By  leveraging  historical  order  data, specifically SKU order frequency, order quantity and dimensional constraints, this study seeks to develop a storage assignment optimization model that enhances picking efficiency and operational performance.

The primary objective of this research is to develop an effective SKU allocation strategy  for  Robotic  Mobile  Fulfillment  Systems  (RMFS)  that  enhances  storage efficiency and order fulfillment performance. Specifically, this study aims to:
1. Increase order throughput by designing a SKU-to-pod assignment approach that reduces pod retrieval delays and supports continuous picking operations.
2. Improve pile-on efficiency by grouping frequently co-ordered SKUs within the same pod to maximize the number of items that can be picked from a single pod visit.
3. Enhance space utilization by applying a categorized storage method that groups SKUs systematically based on order frequency, demand stability, and physical compatibility.
By achieving these goals, this study contributes to the advancement of storage allocation strategies in RMFS environments. It addresses the current research gap in categorized SKU placement and provides practical insights for warehouse managers aiming to improve space usage, fulfillment speed, and overall system efficiency in automated warehouses.

This study is conducted within a defined scope and under specific assumptions, described as follows:
- The primary focus in this study is on small order sizes with multi-item orders typical of e-commerce fulfillment. Large bulk orders are excluded from this study and are assumed to be handled at separate warehouse facilities.
- This study focuses exclusively on the SKU-to-pod assignment policy within warehouse operations. Other key processes, such as order-to-station assignment (POA - Pick Order Assignment) and pod-to-station assignment (PPS - Pick Pod Selection), dynamic replenishment, and robot routing are handled using brute-force methods rather than optimized algorithms.
- The data used for simulation is adapted from actual cases, with the study modeling a total of 7,024 unique SKUs to reflect a realistically large SKU range.
- All SKUs, including those with low demand, are assumed to be stored in the warehouse.  Each  pod  is  designed  with  multiple  compartments,  and  each compartment can contain only a single type of SKU.

- The Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs) modeled in this study are assumed to perform both picking and replenishment tasks. However, the assignment of  of  AMRs  to  specialized  task  are  beyond  the  scope  of  this  work. Additionally, this study does not address the battery charging or management aspects of AMR operations.
- It  is  assumed  that  the  replenishment  station  always  maintains  adequate inventory  levels  to  meet  replenishment  demand,  ensuring  that  SKUs  are always available when required during pod replenishment process.
- The  warehouse  environment  is  modeled  using  an  Agent-Based  Modeling (ABM) approach implemented in NetLogo. The simulation integrates Python
for optimization tasks and uses Excel for data management and storage of simulation results.

This study is organized into five chapters, each addressing a specific aspect of the research process. The organization of the study are as follows:
Chapter 1: Introduction introduces the research topic, background, motivation, objectives, scope, and limitations.
Chapter  2:  Literature  Review  reviews  existing  studies  on  Robotic  Mobile Fulfillment Systems, storage allocation methods, and identifying research gaps.
Chapter  3:  Methodology  describes  the  research  flowchart,  data  collection  and analyzing processes, optimization techniques, and model development approach used in the study.

Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems have emerged as a transformative innovation in warehouse logistics, particularly within the e-commerce sector. Unlike traditional picker-to-parts  systems  where  workers  walk  through  aisles  to  retrieve  items  [23], RMFS follows a parts-to-picker approach, where autonomous mobile robots transport storage units called pods, directly to human-operated or automated picking stations [20]. Several studies have shown that incorporating RMFS into warehouse systems can  significantly  cut  down  picker  travel  time,  making  higher  picking  rates  more doable  compared  to  traditional  warehouse  setups  [24].  Today,  RMFS  is  widely adopted by leading companies such as Alibaba, JD.com, and Cainiao, significantly improving warehouse productivity and cost efficiency [25], [26], [27].
In RMFS, the core components include:

1. Pods: Movable shelves that store various Stock Keeping Units [28]. Each pod consists of multiple compartments designed to hold items of different sizes and categories. A single pod may carry several types of products, depending on the SKU-to-pod assignment strategy adopted. When a pick or replenishment order is generated, the system identifies the appropriate pod(s) containing the required SKUs and instructs a robot to fetch them.
2. Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs): battery-powered robots that are capable of  navigating  warehouse  environments  using  a  grid  of  waypoints  and  predefined  paths  [29].  Each  robot  is  equipped  with  a  lifting  mechanism  that allows  it  to  move  underneath  a  pod,  lift  it,  and  carry  it  to  the  designated workstation [30]. Once the task is completed, the robot returns the pod to an optimized  storage  location  based  on  inventory  rules.  Advanced  RMFS platforms  use  intelligent  robot  scheduling  and  path  planning  algorithms  to avoid congestion, prevent deadlocks, and minimize travel distances.

When  a  customer  order  enters  the  system,  it  is  first  assigned  to  an  available picking  station.  To  fulfill  the  order,  AMRs  are  dispatched  to  retrieve  pods  that contain  the  required  SKUs  from  the  storage  area.  These  pods  are  then  delivered directly  to  the  assigned  picking  station,  allowing  workers  to  efficiently  pick  the necessary items without navigating through warehouse aisles [28]. If the inventory level of a particular SKU within a pod falls below a predefined threshold, the system automatically schedules the pod for replenishment. In such cases, an AMR transports the pod to a replenishment station, where stock levels are restored before the pod is returned to storage or reused for future picking tasks. Merschformann et al. [21] structured the decisions problems in RMFS into several levels  of  warehouse  operation,  with  each  influencing  different  aspects  of  system performance. These decisions are categorized into three main levels: strategic, tactical, and operational, each with distinct objectives and time periods.
Strategic level decisions are made during the construction phase of the warehouse and  have  long-term  implications.  At  this  stage,  one  of  the  key  considerations  is workstation  placement,  which  involves  deciding  where  to  position  picking  and replenishment  stations  in  relation  to  the  storage  area.  Another  important  factor  is storage area dimensioning, which includes determining the overall size of the storage space, how it's divided into zones, and how aisles are arranged.
Tactical  decisions  in  an  RMFS  are  typically  made  at  the  beginning  of  an operational period, such as the start of a workweek, workday or shift. These decisions involve  determining  number  of  pods  per  SKU,  ratio  of  pick  and  replenishment stations, replenishment level, and resource reallocation. These tactical decisions help the  system  stay  agile  and  responsive  to  short-term  changes,  ensuring  smooth operations throughout the day or week.

Operational-level decisions are executed in real time and directly govern the flow of robots, pods, and orders. These are the most dynamic and data-driven decisions in an RMFS and are divided into four main components:

1. Order  Assignment  (OA)  decides  which  station  will  handle  each  incoming order.
2. -Pick  Order  Assignment  (POA):  Assigns  customer  orders  to  picking stations.
3. -Replenishment Order Assignment (ROA): Assigns replenishment tasks to available replenishment stations.
2. Task Creation (TC) involves transforming those assigned orders into specific robot tasks.
5. -Pick Pod Selection (PPS): Choosing which pod to bring to fulfil picking orders.
6. -Replenishment Pod Selection (RPS): Selecting a pod with available space to store incoming inventory
7. -Pod Storage Assignment (PSA): Deciding where to place a pod after it completes a task, with goals of minimizing future travel and balancing access.
3. Task Allocation (TA) deciding where to place a pod after it completes a task, with goals of minimizing future travel and balancing access.
4. Path Planning (PP) deciding where to place a pod after it completes a task, with goals of minimizing future travel and balancing access.

Effectively addressing these decision problems through well-designed rules and coordinated strategies enables RMFS to operate with high efficiency and reliability. Integrated decision-making is essential to optimize throughput, reduce delays, and ensure  timely  and  accurate  order  fulfilment,  ultimately  contributing  to  superior system performance and customer satisfaction.

In  Robotic  Mobile  Fulfillment  Systems,  the  storage  assignment  problem  is  a critical decision problem in tactical level [21], significantly impacting the operational efficiency and throughput of fulfillment operations. It involves assigning SKUs to appropriate  pods  in  a  manner  that  enhances  overall  picking  performance,  reduces robot travel time, and improves system responsiveness. Unlike traditional warehouses where  items  are  placed  in  fixed  racks  and  retrieved  manually,  RMFS  involves dynamic  inventory  storage  and  retrieval  facilitated  by  AMRs,  making  storage decisions more complex and interdependent with system-wide performance factors.

A number of studies have investigated SAP in RMFS settings by focusing on SKU correlation and clustering-based placement strategies. For instance, Kim et al. [33] and Li et al. [34] explored storage assignment strategies that aim to maximize the correlation degree among SKUs, grouping frequently co-ordered items together in the same pods to reduce the number of pod visits per order. Mirzaei et al. [35] expanded on this approach by proposing an integrated cluster allocation policy that accounts for both  item  correlation  and  turnover  rates.  Similarly,  Yang  [36]  emphasized  item similarity as a basis for storage location assignment. However, all the abovementioned studies operate under the constraint that each SKU is assigned to only one pod or group, a design that may limit flexibility and reduce opportunities for optimization under dynamic order scenarios.

In contrast, recent studies have introduced scattered storage as a more flexible and efficient strategy. In this model, a single SKU can be stored across multiple pods, thereby significantly enhance picking efficiency and is suitable for RMFS warehouse. Xiang et al. [37] using historical order data addressed the small-scale item storage assignment problem under the scattered storage method and solved it using a CPLEX solver. Mirzaei  et  al.  [22]  proposed  a  correlated  dispersion  storage  policy  that integrates  SKU  correlation,  turnover  frequency,  and  dispersion  across  pods.  This approach  improves  picking  performance  by  ensuring  that  items  with  high  cooccurrence and turnover rates are accessible from multiple pods without excessive redundancy. Ma et al. [10] added a classification layer, distinguishing between bestselling  and  general-selling  items.  Their  model  incorporated  item  classification alongside  correlation and  scattered storage considerations to  devise  a  more comprehensive storage policy. Zhang et al. [38] further enriched the literature by accounting  for  human  factors.  Their  research  considered  picking  efficiency  and pickers'  physical  effort.  A  more  detailed  comparison  of  previous  studies  on  the storage assignment problem is presented in Table 2.1.

However, despite the valuable contributions, a critical limitation remains across all  the  aforementioned  studies:  they  did  not  explicitly  consider  the  physical dimensions of SKUs and the size constraints of compartments within pods when assigning SKUs to storage locations. In real-world RMFS environments, each pod is divided into compartments with fixed geometrical capacities, and SKUs vary in size and shape. Ignoring these crucial constraints can lead to theoretically optimal storage policies that are infeasible in practice. As such, solutions derived without considering volume fitting, dimension compatibility, and slot availability may not translate well into operational settings. Bridging this gap requires integrating physical feasibility checks into the storage assignment logic to ensure that assigned SKUs can actually be placed in the intended compartments.

Item correlation is widely recognized as a crucial concept in modern warehouse optimization and plays an important role in solving the storage assignment problem within Robotic Mobile  Fulfillment Systems.  As  highlighted in the previous subchapter, many recent studies (see Table 2.1) use item correlation to improve SKUto-pod assignment strategies. When products with high correlation are placed together within the same pod, they are more likely to be appeared together in a single order [41]. This increases the number of items that can be retrieved in a single pod trip, thereby  reducing  the  overall  number  of  pod  visits  required  to  complete  order fulfillment.
By understanding how products are frequently ordered together, researchers and practitioners  can  identify  meaningful  relationships  that  helps  clustering,  scattered storage policies, and mixed storage configurations. This data-driven perspective helps RMFS warehouses boost picking efficiency, reduce unnecessary robot travel, and adapt dynamically to changing demand patterns.

Market  Basket  Analysis  is  one  of  the  most  widely  applied  techniques  for uncovering these item relationships that associated with customer buying behaviour [42]. MBA relies on Association Rule Mining to analyze transaction data, detecting which  items  appear  together  in  customer  orders.  Studies  such  as  Ünvan  [43] demonstrate that robust algorithms like Apriori and FP-Growth can effectively reveal strong correlations between SKUs. These patterns can then be used to group items with high co-occurrence, ultimately improving layout and storage allocation decisions in practice.
The  strategic  impact  of  understanding  item  correlation  extends  beyond  simple pairings.  Kumar  et  al.  [44]  emphasize  that  recognizing  hidden  interdependencies among SKUs enables companies to design smarter replenishment rules and crossselling  opportunities,  while  Sajwan  and  Tripathi  [45]  show  that  a  comprehensive MBA framework can illuminate the more complex interdependencies in shopping baskets,  allowing  companies  to  tailor  promotions,  manage  stock  levels,  and  even redesign store layouts to reflect actual buying behavior. Their study underscores the potential of ARM for generating strategic business insights, rather than treating it solely as a technical data mining task.

In the context of RMFS, association rules hold particular value for SKU-to-pod assignment and storage design. By identifying frequently co-ordered items, warehouse managers can cluster highly correlated SKUs within the same pods or strategically  disperse  them  to  balance  picking  efficiency  and  travel  distance.  The insights gained through ARM thus align closely with broader warehouse optimization goals, including increase order throughput and pile-on.

Effective SKU classification is a fundamental component in optimizing storage strategies within RMFS. As modern warehouses handle thousands of diverse SKUs with  varying  demand  patterns,  dimensions,  and  turnover  rates,  classifying  SKUs appropriately enables more intelligent decisions in storage assignment, order picking, and replenishment planning. By grouping SKUs based on shared attributes such as demand frequency, volatility, or co-occurrence in orders, RMFS can achieve higher picking efficiency and reduce unnecessary pod movements.

Several  studies  have  highlighted  the  importance  of  SKU  classification  in improving warehouse performance, such as reduce pick travel distance and enhance throughput.    Yuan  et  al.  [46]  investigated  pod  assignment  strategies  in  RMFS  by comparing  random,  class-based,  and  turnover-based  approaches.  Their  findings indicate that class-based storage using two or three categories captures most of the potential advantages, with having more variation. Muppani and Adil [13] demonstrated that implementing a class-based storage policy, which groups SKUs with similar demand patterns, can reduce both order picking distance and required storage space. This approach improves space utilization and helps ensure that highturnover products are stored in more accessible locations. Another study by Mirzaei et  al.  [22]  demonstrated  that  combining  turnover-based,  correlation-based,  and dispersed storage strategies in robotic warehouses can lead to significant cost savings and  reduce  operational  time.  By  aligning  SKU  placement  with  both  demand frequency and product correlations, and distributing inventory across multiple pods, warehouses  can  reduce  retrieval  effort,  limit  pod  congestion,  and  improve  order fulfillment efficiency. This integrated approach minimizes unnecessary robot travel and redundant handling, resulting in lower operational costs.

In  order  to  effectively  manage  inventory  and  improve  storage  assignment  in Robotic Mobile Fulfilment Systems, it is important to recognize that not all SKUs behave the same in terms of demand. One way to capture this variability is through the  Coefficient  of  Variation,  a  statistical  measure  that  measures  the  ratio  of  the standard deviation to the mean of a data set [47]. The coefficient of variation is widely used across various fields such as agriculture, industry, healthcare, social sciences, and education, serving multiple research and analytical purposes [48]. In the context of  inventory  and  warehouse management, CV serves as a normalized indicator to quantify  the  volatility  of  SKU  demand,  providing  a  solid  foundation  for  setting differentiated inventory and storage allocation policy.
In an  RMFS  environment,  where  storage  space  is  mobile  and  dynamic, understanding the volatility of SKU demand is essential for optimizing SKU-to-pod assignments. This study applies CV as a decision variable to determine the inventory service level and the dispersion strategy for each SKU. SKUs with low CV values typically  show  stable  and  predictable  demand.  In  contrast,  SKUs  with  higher  CV values tend to display irregular or intermittent demand.

The  relevance  of  using  CV  for  classification  has  been  well-established  across various fields.  For  example,  the  ABC-XYZ  classification  framework,  which combines demand quantity (ABC) with demand variability (XYZ), applies the CV as a core measure to distinguish between stable (X class), moderately variable (Y-class), and highly erratic (Z class) items [49]. This combined approach helps companies align their inventory control and replenishment strategies with the real patterns of order.
Beyond warehousing, the value of CV as a simple yet robust analytical tools has also been demonstrated in fields such as agricultural monitoring, where it was used to classify cropland areas across diverse climates based on temporal backscatter data [50].  Taken  together,  these  examples  highlight  that  integrating  CV  into  SKU analytical tools enables more responsive, data-driven storage and inventory decisions, ultimately  supporting  higher  picking  efficiency  and  system  throughput  in  RMFS operations.

This  study  combines  K-Means  clustering  and  Elbow  method  to  determine  the number of SKU classes. K-means is a clustering algorithm that partitions data into K distinct groups by minimizing the distance between each data point and the center (centroid) of its assigned cluster [55]. Before applying the K-means algorithm, one important consideration is selecting an appropriate value for the number of clusters (K). One commonly used technique for determining this value is the Elbow method.
The elbow method identifies the optimal K by analyzing a graph that plots the Within-Clusters Sum of Squared (WCSS) against different K values (see Equation (34)) [56]. The ideal point is typically located at the "elbow" of the curve, where the SSE begins to level off. This point represents the best number of clusters to use.

In this study, three product mixture scenarios are considered to evaluate the impact of different allocation strategies on system performance:

The  random  mixture  strategy  is  implemented  as  the  baseline  for  SKU  to  pod assignment.  SKUs  are  distributed  randomly  across  available  pods  without considering  their  demand  classification.  In  many  studies,  Random  Storage Assignment  Policy  (RSAP)  is  regarded  as  a  reference  point  for  assessing alternative allocation strategies [10]. This neutral setup provides a reference point for comparing the effectiveness of more structured SKU placement methods.

Each  pod  is  assigned  SKUs  belonging  to  a  single  classification  group.  This method  aims  to  align picking operations with SKU  stability, potentially simplifying replenishment and retrieval processes.

Each  pod  contains  a  mix  of  SKUs  from  different  classification  groups.  This diversified allocation increases the probability that a single pod can fulfill a wider range of order lines, thereby improving the pile-on rate and reducing the total number of pod movements required for order fulfillment.
By analyzing these three SKU mixture scenarios, this study aims to identify the configuration that best balances inventory management complexity with operational efficiency, ultimately supporting higher throughput and pile-on.

In this study, dimensional constraints are explicitly applied to ensure that the SKU to compartment assignment is physically feasible and operationally realistic. In real RMFS  operations,  pods  are  divided  into  compartments  with  fixed  geometrical capacities, and SKUs vary significantly in their dimensions and packaging shapes. By applying dimensional constraints during the storage assignment process, the system aims to achieve more compact SKU allocation, thereby minimizing the total number of pods required to satisfy inventory requirements.
A structured procedure is implemented to identify the optimal placement of SKUs and to determine the most suitable pod and compartment type, while ensuring that dimensional constraints are satisfied:

1. Dimension sorting: each SKU's and compartment's dimensions are sorted into longest, second longest, and shortest sides. This standardization ensures consistent orientation when evaluating fit within compartments.
2. Fit assessment: for each SKU, the fit is checked across five predefined types of compartments. The maximum  quantity that can be stored within each compartment type is then calculated based on the SKU's physical dimensions and the capacity of the compartment.
3. Maximum capacity  and  inventory  level  comparison:  the  calculated  maximum capacity for each SKU to compartment pair is compared with the SKU's minimum required  inventory  level.  This  comparison  ensures  that  the  selected  storage
configuration  can  support  operational  replenishment  needs  without  exceeding compartment constraints.

Scattered or dispersed storage has been widely recognized in the literature as an effective approach  to enhance  picking efficiency  in  warehouse  systems.  By distributing SKUs across multiple storage locations or pods, the likelihood of having required items closer to pick stations increases, thereby reducing travel distances and improving system responsiveness. As summarized in Chapter 2, Table 2.1, several studies  have  demonstrated  that  this  strategy  is  especially  beneficial  in  RMFS warehouse.
In this study, SKU dispersion is implemented based on the CV of each SKU's order  frequency.  The  CV  serves  as  a  normalized  measure  of  demand  variability, offering  a  standardized  basis  for  determining  how  widely  each  SKU  should  be distributed within the storage system. A higher CV indicates greater variability and unpredictability in order patterns, while a lower CV suggests more stable, consistent demand.

SKUs with high CV values are dispersed across a larger number of pods. This strategy increases the chances that SKUs whose demand patterns are sporadic, are available when needed, improving the system's responsiveness and reducing the risk of  pod  unavailability.  In  contrast,  SKUs  with  low  CV  values  exhibit  stable  and predictable demand and are therefore assigned to fewer pods to save storage space and avoids storing the same items unnecessarily.

The Storage Area constitutes the largest section of the layout and accommodates Pods when they are not actively involved in picking or replenishment tasks. The rapid rise of Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems has introduced numerous decision-making challenges aimed at improving order fulfillment efficiency. Among these, the optimization of the Storage Assignment Problem (SAP) has emerged as a critical  concern,  as  it  directly  affects  warehouse  performance.  While  a  variety  of performance  metrics  have  been  proposed  to  evaluate  SKU  allocation  strategies, maximizing throughput remains the main goal across all warehouse operations. Most research on SAP has primarily emphasized SKU correlation and item classification methods, which are indeed important for formulating allocation policies. However, such approaches often assume the presence of strong SKU relationships, which is not always the case in every warehouse. However, despite the valuable contributions, a critical  research  gap  remains  across  previous  studies,  they  did  not  consider  the physical dimensions of SKUs and the size constraints of compartments within pods when assigning SKUs to storage locations.

In this study, we proposed a SKU-to-pod allocation strategy specifically designed for RMFS warehouses, incorporating several key operational factors such as order frequency, product turnover rates, product correlation, and dimensional constraints. Our approach began with a systematic analysis of historical order data to classify SKUs  based  on  demand  frequency  and  stability.  We  proposed  two  SKU-to-pod policies  based  on  this  SKUs  classification:  one  pod  one  class  policy  and  one  pod mixed class policy, we then compared these two allocation policies with the random policy  baseline.  To  evaluate  the  real-world  applicability  of  the  proposed  policies, dimensional constraints were applied to all three scenarios. Furthermore, a dispersion policy was introduced to investigate the effect of distributing SKUs across multiple pods, thereby increasing SKU accessibility.  A simulation model was developed using NetLogo for agent-based modeling and Python for optimization, and performance was evaluated using a dataset of 7,024 SKUs.

Simulation results showed that under dimensional constraints alone, the One Pod Mixed  Class  strategy  achieved  the  best  performance,  with  mean  throughput  of 91.90%  and  mean  pile-on  of  9.79,  followed  by  One  Pod  One  Class  with  mean throughput of 85.23% and mean pile-on of 9.37 and the Random baseline with mean

throughput of 78.65% and mean pile-on of 7.35. After applying the dispersion policy, both metrics improved across all scenarios. Mix Class scenario throughput increased to 99.22%, One Class scenario to 96.22%, and Random scenario to 79.93%, while pile-on rose to 9.96, 9.75, and 7.46, respectively. These gains coincide with greater storage  usage  from  roughly  273  to  472  pods,  reflecting  the  trade-off  between dispersion and pod capacity requirements.
Hypothesis  testing  using  ANOVA  confirmed  significant  differences  in  both throughput and pile-on across all scenarios under dimensional constraints and under the dispersion policy (p < 0.05). Paired t-tests further verified that introducing the dispersion policy led to statistically significant improvements in throughput and pileon for all three allocation strategies (p < 0.05).  These results validate the effectiveness of  SKU  classification  by  demand  frequency  and  stability,  and  demonstrate  that dispersion can further enhance performance by increasing SKU accessibility, while also highlighting the importance of considering physical storage constraints in realworld RMFS optimization.

While this study has successfully proposed  a structured SKU-to-pod allocation policy and demonstrated significant improvements in both throughput and pile-on performance, several directions remain open for future exploration to further enhance RMFS operations.
The  current  classification  framework  is  primarily  based  on  demand  stability. However,  additional  factors  such  as  SKU  physical  size,  weight,  and  handling complexity  could  be  integrated  into  the  classification  criteria  to  create  more comprehensive storage profiles.
Future research could incorporate pod weight balancing when designing SKU-topod assignment policies. Uneven weight distribution within pods may increase the mechanical  burden  on  AMRs  and  negatively  affect  battery  efficiency  and  energy consumption. Introducing a weighted balancing constraint during SKU assignment could help ensure pod stability and improve the energy consumption of AMRs.
Continuing from previous recommendation, energy consumption is an increasingly important performance metric in modern warehouse systems. While this study focused on throughput and pile-on, future work could evaluate strategies based on energy efficiency, such as minimizing total robot travel distance or power usage, thus aligning system design with sustainability goals.

Finally,  a  promising  area  lies  in  developing  dynamic  SKU-to-pod  policies  that adapt in real time to changing demand patterns. As product lifecycles shorten and customer  preferences  fluctuate,  integrating  predictive  analytics  or  reinforcement learning,  future  systems  can  reconfigure  SKU  placements  periodically,  ensuring sustained efficiency under evolving operational conditions.
In  summary,  while  this  research  has  laid  a  solid  foundation  for  a  feasible  and effective  SKU  allocation  policy  in  RMFS,  future  enhancements  that  incorporate product-specific attributes, energy efficiency metrics, and real-time adaptability hold great potential to advance the state-of-the-art in intelligent warehouse automation. By building upon the groundwork established in this study and exploring the proposed extensions, future research can further drive the evolution of RMFS and contribute meaningfully to broader innovations in automated warehouse management.
